title: The Value of Free Water: Analyzing South Africa's Free Basic Water Policy
summary_en: South Africa's 'Free Basic Water' policy gives every household a 6-kilolitre free monthly water allowance — the WHO recommended minimum. Szabó structurally estimates household water demand around the kink at the 6-kilolitre threshold and finds that the free block does little to lower poor households' total water bills (they consume well above 6 kl) and substantially raises water use among middle-income households (a Giffen-style block-pricing distortion). A means-tested cash transfer would deliver the same welfare with much less water and cheaper public outlay.
data_used: Household-level micro-data on metered water consumption from a South African municipality, with full block-tariff information and household demographics. Structural demand estimation accounts for nonlinear pricing kinks at the free-block threshold.
policy_relevance: Direct relevance for Hungarian energy and utilities policy (energiaár-támogatás, rezsicsökkentés, district-heating tariffs): the paper formalises why universal free-block tariffs are dominated by means-tested cash transfers when the free block sits below typical household consumption. For Hungarian energy-poverty policy considering or extending universal-allowance schemes, results argue for moving the policy toward direct income support of vulnerable households.
